title: Paraiba Tourmaline
author: David Federman
excerpt: The world has lived so long with a six-digit Dow Jones figure that it comes as a shock to be reminded this bellwether index didn't top 1,500 until 1983. Now imagine the reaction of sound minds when quoted prices of more than $20,000 per carat for tourmaline. Paraiba tourmalines are magnificent by any measure, sporting electric teal and sapphire-blue colors that make them ravishingly distinctive.
content:
The world has lived so long with a six-digit Dow Jones figure that it comes as a shock to be reminded this bellwetter index for the U.S. stock market didn’t top 1,500 until 1983 and 2,000 until 1986. And when you are told that the average sank to 577 in 1973 during a recession far milder than that of 1990-92, your brain feels like a gong in a Buddhist monastery. Numbers that low are just too bad to be true.

Now imagine the reaction of sound minds when quoted prices of more than $20,000 per carat for tourmaline. Of course, these prices are commanded not by an ordinary garden variety fine tourmaline. No this altitude is reserved exclusively for Paraiba tourmaline: a strain of neon-glowing tourmalines from Brazil’s Paraiba mining district discovered in 1989. Numbers that high were unheard of for so-called semi-precious gemstones in the past.

Paraiba prices are as close to paranormal as gem prices get. They have defied gravity, conventional wisdom and a blistering recession in the most important market for premium gemstones, Japan — any one of which should have kept prices pinned down to four digits, like other tourmalines.

Granted, Paraiba tourmalines are magnificent by any measure, sporting at their best electric teal and sapphire-blue colors that make them ravishingly distinctive.

Natural Selection

When dealers first saw samples of the new-find tourmalines in early 1989, the vibrant colors left them as much in awe as in doubt. Dealers thought that colors that vivid couldn’t possibly be natural. Given the possibility that a significant percentage of pink and red tourmalines are irradiated, stones from Paraiba were bound to trigger trade skepticism. Endowed with colors that evoked comparisons to peacock feathers and tropical fish, the colors just seemed too good to be true.

Finally, gemologists who studied the material concluded its colors were, for the most part, natural — the product of the trace element copper. We say “for the most part” because Brazilian dealers admit heating some sapphire-blue, as well as gray and dark-green stones, to render them spectacular turquoise and tsavorite hues.

Once Paraiba tourmaline was given a clean bill of health, holdouts began buying it. At first, its mile-high prices reflected newness and overnight celebrity status. In time, they reflected profound regard for this material. And not just fine large gems, but small stones were highly sought. Designers discovered that adding just one or two tiny Paraiba tourmalines to accent a piece gave it enough extra appeal to more than justify paying the very high prices asked for it.

Paraiba’s Palette

title: Maine Tourmaline
author: Brecken Branstrator, GIA GG
excerpt: Tourmaline was first discovered in the Mt. Mica area in southwestern Maine in 1820. Maine tourmaline ranges in color from black to vibrant shades of pink, red, green, and blue, as well as the popular “watermelon” variety, and its fine qualities can rival those from localities such as California, Brazil, or Nigeria.
content:
Tourmaline was first discovered in the Mt. Mica area in southwestern Maine in 1820. Several other deposits have been found across the state since then, with the gem becoming so important to the state’s history and identity that it was named Maine’s state mineral. It has been beloved by the gem community and locals alike since.

Maine tourmaline ranges in color from black to the vibrant shades of pink/red, green, and blue the gem is known for, as well as the popular “watermelon” variety, and its fine qualities can rival those from localities such as California, Brazil, or Nigeria.

According to Maine.gov, the most common species in the state is schorl, a black, iron-bearing tourmaline. Less common but still present is elbaite, which produces the more colorful varieties. The finest specimens in Maine are found in pegmatites, which offer pockets that allow for larger crystals to grow.

Three Things to Know About Maine Tourmaline

The Hamlin Necklace: One of the most significant pieces of North American jewelry features Maine tourmaline. Augustus Hamlin commissioned the piece to showcase tourmalines uncovered at the Mt. Mica mine he owned. The necklace consists of 18 removable pendants with tourmalines of various colors and beryl from Mount Mica attached to a simple gold chain, with the central pendant featuring a 34.25-carat tourmaline. It was bequeathed to the Harvard Mineralogical Museum in 1934.

The Big Find: The 1972 discovery of huge pockets of tourmaline of all colors at a mine on Plumbago Mountain in Newry, Maine. Over two years, it yielded more than a ton of tourmaline, marking North America’s largest and most significant gem-quality tourmaline discovery, putting Maine firmly on the gemological map and reawakening gem mining across the state.

Pricing: Maine tourmaline, because of its rarity, beauty, and significance to the state, can have a premium when it comes to pricing. Local collectors and gem connoisseurs may be willing to pay those prices for a fine piece, but as the stone is best known to a smaller group of people, it could see some price resistance in the larger market if priced too high.

title: When Gemstones Are Waste
author: Kerry Gregory, GIA GG, FGA
excerpt: Many industry organizations are against the use of the term “recycled” when it comes to gemstones, but the author argues that there are myriad situations where the term could be accurately applied. From mining tailings to pawnbroker vaults, gemstones enter the waste stream at every stage of the pipeline.
content:
Many industry organizations are against use of the term “recycled” when it comes to gemstones, but the author argues that there are myriad situations where the term could be accurately applied, even if she has no plans to take up the charge to change their minds.

Ever since I was a child, I have loved to argue. I don’t mean in the sense of “having a fight,” but in the scientific sense of exploring arguments, presenting data, asking questions, and having other people discuss, refute, agree, or otherwise, until one of us has proven our point (or we agree to disagree). It has always come from a point of curiosity, of learning, of research and wanting to find the answer or find what is right.

The term “recycled,” when used in conjunction with gemstones, is contentious in the trade. Both the American Gem Trade Association (AGTA) and Jewelers Vigilance Committee (JVC) have called for the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to ban the use of the term in relation to gemstones.

Defining Waste and Recycling

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) defines waste as “any garbage or refuse, sludge from a wastewater treatment plant, water supply treatment plant, or air pollution control facility and other discarded material, resulting from industrial, commercial, mining, and agricultural operations, and from community activities.”

“Recycling” is defined by the EPA as “the process of collecting and processing materials that would otherwise be thrown away as trash and turning them into new products.” In U.K. regulations, it is “any recovery operation by which waste materials are reprocessed into products, materials, or substances, whether for their original purpose or other purpose.”

Where Gemstones Become Waste

In mining, we have gem material that is broken, too small, or too low-quality to be economically viable to a miner or mining company. These get discarded in tailings or are otherwise overlooked. In gem cutting, we produce offcuts and dust. These by-products often will not get used and instead will be discarded. Stones can get broken during the process.

I know many stone dealers who, if they drop a particularly low value gemstone on the office floor and do not find it immediately, will not bother to look for it. It is not worth their time or money. In this case, they are effectively “abandoning” the stone.

In retail, there are instances where even fully manufactured items need to be “disposed” of—faulty items returned for refund, stock that gets damaged in inventory, and excess inventory that is unsold. These items will mostly be “recycled”—repaired, reworked, or scrapped—and most if not all of the materials reused.

We also have “burden” (similar to residue), materials that are unsuitable, unwanted, surplus to requirements, or even outside the scope of the holder’s expertise. This is a regular occurrence in the gold buying or pawnbroking businesses. Money is made in trading in the commodity of the precious metal. Often little or no fiscal value is given for colored gemstones and commonly not even diamonds.

If we can take any of the gems from any part of this waste stream, whether those are tailings from mining or bashed up gems from pawnbrokers, process them in a way that adds value, and use them in some way, surely these are recycled gemstones by the legislative definitions of both waste and recycling?

About the Author: Kerry Gregory is known for her presentations and hands-on gemology workshops. She has had numerous articles on practical gemology published in both U.K. and U.S. publications. A past tutor and head of ATC for Gem-A, she served on the board of Gem-A and ran one of the U.K. branches.
